questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Academic opportunities

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: Berkeley is one of the most well known and highly renowned universities throughout the world and is top tier on almost every ranking out there. Combined with the unique placement close to San Francisco and a variety of interesting cities, nature, the ocean and national parks it offers everything you could imagine and dream of. The prestige itself was the major reason for choosing the university as it looks amazing on your CV, however the course selection, professors and in general the opportunities that UC Berkeley presents are just amazing

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer:
UC Berkeley is in general a great place. The academics are as you would expect (don't be scared  - it isn't as intimidating and scary as it seems). The people are welcoming, the weather is great and the opportunities to go on weekend trips are fantastic. The only thing that draws me down to a 9/10 score is the number of homeless people and the crime rates. This is in no way unique to UC Berkeley however it does dampen the excitement a bit, and you should be prepared to take a Uber home from parties - the US has a different security level than EU no matter where you go. 

When that is said I hardly ever experienced anything unusual/uncomfortable that you wouldn't in Copenhagen. A highlight is definitely the people, the weekend trips and the overall experience of being at one of the most beautiful campus' on the planet with world famous scientists wondering the same paths as yourself.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Very easy - UC Berkeley sends a lot(!) of informational e-mails, updates, recommendations and random links before you even set foot on the plane. This can be a bit overwhelming at times however a common sense for which e-mails are relevant and which are not will pull you through just fine. The UCEAP website offers a lot of guiding in when to apply for courses, where to get information and how to proceed. Be prepared for the high amount of bureaucracy that is a part of the US culture - fear not, if you by accident contact the "wrong" person they will happily assist you and try to help you towards the right places.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: Obviously someone won't greet you at San Francisco airport with a sign saying "Welcome XX". When you arrive (especially if you arrive some time before the semester starts) it might even feel like a vacation. I would recommend arriving some time before start to let yourself fall into place, get to know your neighborhood, find out where you like to shop for groceries, meet some of the other people attending the university and get a normal life going. This might even be a good time to bond with a few of the Danes which might help you build relations to other international and American people later on as they probably don't attend the same courses as you.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer:
I was pretty satisfied, however the "Golden Bear Orientation" (GBO) feels a bit long and unnecessary at times. You will be grouped with random transfer students which means that a low of information might not be relevant as an exchange student. When that is said you should definitely attend the first coupe of days and see if you like it - give everyone and everything a chance, but be prepared to also plan something yourself. A lot of the students are under 21 which means they can't get into bars/pubs. As expected UC Berkeley also does not condone drinking during orientation which is great but might also put a damper on the social activities (Us Danes are just better as socializing with a beer or 2). When that is said I did attend during the pandemic so it was a mix of online and in-person activities which might have affected the program. 
You WILL be "forced" to do a number of online programs about alcohol, drugs, sex, mental health, relationships (you name it - they have it). This might feel comical and ridiculous at times - and it probably is. This is targeted new American students who might only be 17-18 years old and be moving out and living on their own for the first time. Therefore, it is not always relevant as an international student - but once again, it is an experience and certainly brings out some laughs and smiles along the way.

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: It is "pretty" easy to find housing on your own. There are several Facebook groups that offers housing. Along this there is the offers from the University where you can apply to I-house, Co-ops etc. Go on craigs-list, message some other Danes about what their plans are and just google "Berkeley housing" and utilize the many possibilities there are. Be aware of scammers and preferably don't pay any deposit before you at least have had a zoom meeting or examined the housing yourself.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: It is damn expensive. No matter what you should be prepared to pay at least 1000-2000 USD per month. Personally I found a private room in a house for 1400 USD which is pretty "cheap" compared to some other places. Definitely try to find housing with other students as this will increase your chances of bonding with new people and just engage you more in social life on an everyday basis.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer:
It IS expensive - there is no way around it. It's the Bay area in the most expensive US state. Think about if you prefer to share a room, be in a co-op and how much of your budget you are willing to spend. 

I have seen and heard people say that you should never bike in the US and to campus. This is certainly not true, I bought a bike of FB market place for 200 Bucks and used it with pleasure all semester. Get a great bike lock (bikes do get stolen like in CPH), buy a helmet and use your common sense - I rode my bike home from parties on several occasions without problems just be aware of your surroundings and don't expect American people in their big cars to hold back for bicycles.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: It is VERY simple and logical to sign up for courses. Furthermore UC Berkeley has a great system for course selection both for lectures and discussion sections where you can tailor your school schedule. It is also very easy to change courses during the semester as they have a "drop period".

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: They have a portal called "Calnet" where you signup for classes using the prefixes and number e.g. "MCB153". You can basically add the courses and try and tailor your schedule before the sign-up begins by adding them to your basket - so when the actual sign-up starts you just press a button to add the courses from your basket and you are signed up. Do yourself a favor and go on Youtube and search for UC Berkeley course signup or something like that. There are so many 5-10 minute videos showing the system and it is honestly a better sign-up system than UCPH.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: Multiple advisors on Campus are available - as mentioned Youtube is a great option as well. Just click around the site before the whole sign-up stress starts and do your "Homework" before hand. You can also e-mail some professors for special registration keys, however not all courses allow for this but it certainly does not harm you.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: Very successful. I got 4/4 classes that I wanted and then I later without problems changes 2 of my courses to some other courses. A quick tip is that a few weeks before semester start different "DeCals" will be published. They are basically student run courses with guest lectures that normally account for 1-2 credits. These are great if you just need that final 1 credit to reach the minimum required for a semester.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Don't panic if you are not enrolled in all the courses you want. The drop period is used by almost all students to switch classes and Berkeley is very flexible with switching classes. You can even go to the first lecture even if you are on the waiting list and talk to the professor after class about the possibility to enroll. Mention that you are very interested in the class, that you are an international student and they might even bump you up in the queue - they might even directly add you and expand the class with a few people extra depending on the demand.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I was overall pretty satisfied. Some other KU "reviews" of Berkeley might be a bit daunting and intimidating as it is often said that the level of academics is higher than at UCPH. I found that it is pretty much the same level, they do however have a lot more focus on research than in Denmark. The instructors, professors and GSI's all want you to succeed and will happily help. Be prepared to be challenged as you would in DK and yes it might be harder to follow the lectures as they are all in English no matter how proficient your abilities are. However, the joy of being taught by Nobel Laurates and world leading scientists and researchers will make it all worth it. I put 4/5 as the exams are mostly MC which might make it a bit too easy compared to the level taught in class (This is of course also a positive thing as you don't necessarily have to understand 100% of the material being taught). I just think that they should challenge the students with more creative thinking and problem solving. However again - this is due to the cultural differences between the US and EU - take it as an experience and enjoy some extra points you might not deserve.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: Once again - don't be scared about the reputation of UC Berkeley, you will probably perform at the same level as in Copenhagen as long as you attend lectures and put in a normal amount of work.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: They have a lot more guest lectures that present on their own research - this might at times be very high level as it is the world leading research that might even be nominated for a Nobel prize in years to come. Fear not, the professors and GSI's know when the material is "over" the expected level of competencies for Undergraduates and they will accommodate this in the midterms, quizzes, exams etc.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
BIOE115 - Tissue Engineering
IB118 - Organismal Microbiomes and Host-Pathogen Interactions
MCB153 - Molecular Therapeutics
MCB198 - CRISPR: Basic Principles and Applications

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: MCB153 and IB118. MCB153 is a new course from UC Berkeley and is focused on a variety of different diseases and general issues with the human body and how to tackle, target and drug them. The course is very focused around research and how to bridge the gap between academia and a finished "product" i.e. a drug/medicine to treat the disease that basic research tries to understand. The professors Andrew Dillin and Sarah Stanley are both experts within their fields of work and through their long career has a broad knowledge of other researchers. These are often invited to guest lecture including a number of Nobel Prize winners. The course encourages discussion between students and researchers and is a pleasant learning environment. IB118 has many characteristics of a Microbiology/Immunology course from Copenhagen but also goes beyond standard text-book knowledge and presents cutting edge research.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: Insurance is expensive! Also weekend trips might be an unexpected cost - however it is totally worth it because you get to see California and bond with the other people on the trip so definitely worth it.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Again housing and insurance is just expensive in California. Alcohol on clubs and bars are the same price as Copenhagen.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: You can basically engage in every activity that you want. They have endless clubs, sports etc. If you have the time you should participate in at least 1, remember that fitness/gym is free and also a great activity to do with your new found friends.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Every single one you can imagine. Go to the sporting activities (UC Berkeley American football, water polo, basketball, volleyball, tennis). The facilities are amazing considering that you are watching college sports and the atmosphere and collectiveness is wonderful to experience.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Sports - see above.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Yosemite, Las Vegas, Monterey Bay, San Francisco (Golden gate, Alcatraz etc.), Grand Canyon, Go to the Football game VS Stanford.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Pretty easily - the US culture is not much different from that in EU and Denmark in general. Be open minded and talk to people - try and engage in conversation and don't be passive.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Be mindful and respective of other cultures, have an open mind and heart. In the start of the exchange try not to say no to anything or anyone. People will be making social arrangements a lot in the beginning and it is important to participate to find the right group of friends. With that said, later on it is okay to be picky and reject some "offers" to hang out.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: Not really anything in particular

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: The social activities even when these include going to bars and restaurants where you might go above your budget. U really enjoyed the weekend trips even though they are expensive.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer: Everything is listed above

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Everything is listed above

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: The academics, the social life and the weekend trips.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Adapting to the time difference and the fact you are on the other side of the world while your family, friends and loved ones are at home.

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: No

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
